journal.text: It is perhaps fitting that the first pieces of rune equipment were worn by the creator of runes themselves, Guthix. Of course, rune metal is not made of runes, and indeed has no actual connection to runes at all, but Guthix, for all his many qualities, was not the greatest of wordsmiths. The god journeyed deep into Ashenfall, where he discovered the Wellspring and the strange metal that glistened nearby from the rocks. It has a soft blue-ish hue that was both subtle and entrancing in different ways and he became intrigued. Using techniques he had learned from the dwarves, Guthix attempted to fashion the metal into equipment, yet it resisted his every effort and refused to be anything more than a strange, glittery sort of ore. There was magic there, in the ore. It resisted pickaxes, it repelled weaponry, it practically jeered at Guthix, telling him that it was the most interesting metal around. Yet no matter what he tried, he could not tame it. Until he discovered luminite, and then everything changed.

journal.text: If you fancy a giggle, watch an amateur try to mine runite. Grab a chair, pull yourself a dwarven stout, and watch the carnage. Runite, you see, actively repels a pickaxe. It twinkles with magic, and that magic - perhaps through some kind of geological evolutionary step - resists any attempt to mine it. Artlessly swing a pickaxe at a clump of runite and the pickaxe will bounce backwards, boomeranging towards the miner's head. There's a reason why field medics are posted at dwarven mines. The secret is that runite is soft. Not as soft as clay or gold, perhaps, but softer than most metals. You don't need to swing your pickaxe hard or fast. All that is needed is some finesse and patience. Better still, a runite pickaxe will disrupt the magical fields around the ore, pushing the ore out of the rock.

She would leap into the black dragon nests, lop off a head with her rune greatsword and then boil the head in a kitchen pot. Kuldra felt that The Muggathug was encroaching on her territory. She commanded that The Muggathug attended her, before she bit off The Muggathug's head, boiled it in a mixture of ice and fire, and tasked her smiths with making a ring for her. You don't want to be aiming at a garou berserker, only to watch the arrow arc away from them. As Vannaka would say, 'your problem is that you're thinking like an amateur'. Archers don't actually WANT arrows to hit other metals: they want to slip into the gaps between armour, puncturing an armpit or neck. The best archers also love a trick-shot, hitting an opponent through a sea of allies. The trick is to use the diamagnetism to your benefit, and that - again, to quote Vannaka - 'comes from the hardest skill of all. Practice'.

journal.text: In Brynmoor, the wand will forever be associated with Holly Arnuld. She applied to every wizard to become their apprentice, but was turned down on account of her having a single arm. She would craft runes and concoct potions, displaying her skill and speed - faster than most other apprentices. The wizards would fill their eyes with pity and put a hand to her shoulder. "But can you hold a staff, lassie?", they would say. "I need to know that I can rely on you for all things." Holly would not wield a staff. She believed them to be showy and unnecessary. They were as performative as a peacock's tail. Instead, she kept a sliver of staff in her sleeve. This was her ash wand, discretely socketed and ready. She found work as a scullery maid for a noblewoman. She was travelling in their entourage when they were attacked by enough goblins to overwhelm the guards. The goblins were on the brink of killing the noblewoman when Holly pulled her wand from the stitching in her sleeve. She whipped the goblins from their feet with air magic. Every time they tried to get back on their feet, she put them to the floor again. They stumbled and stood, stumbled and stood, until finally she tumbled them off a cliff. Holly was given a full purse and the contacts of a friend of the nobelwoman. She was enrolled in a school of magic. Her specialism? Well, she put all her efforts into the merit of wands.

journal.text: There was a room in the Brynmoor School of Magic that every new student visited at least once. The students' purposes differed, of course: some students wanted to see if it was merely myth; others wanted to simply observe it; a few wanted to go a little further... The room was Arnuld's Sanctum. In the centre of the circular room was a single pedestal with an oak wand. From a distance, it looked like it floated, but step closer and it would be clear that it was supported with a stand of glass. There were no inscriptions on the pedestal, no decorations on the walls. The room lacked any detailing, outside of a single sprig of holly, etched onto the lower-half of the wand. No one had been able to grasp the oak wand to take it. Any fool who tried would be overcome by the sensation that they were on fire. They would drop to the floor, contorting in an effort to remove flames that were not there. Only the stupid and self-worthy would attempt it, and there was always a crowd of third- and fourth-years to watch and laugh at them. When the School of Magic fell to fire (which had nothing to do with the wand), no one had the presence of mind to visit the Sanctum. Fire surged up the pedestal, and the wand's magical protection dropped. Embracing the fire, the wand was consumed, as if it were finally with its own kind. Then the pedestal dropped and something opened.

journal.text: Holly Arnuld travelled the world in search of materials for her wands. She would freely talk about the misadventures - making wands out of jade vines, for one - but would rarely talk about her successes. It was hard to know whether she was humble or unwilling to reveal her secrets. One of those misadventures was in Bloodblight. She found a tree in the swamps with twigs that looked uncannily like wands. She wouldn't need to process the twigs much beyond snapping them from the tree. They glowed with magic, as if already prepared for their role. Holly would treat this as a lesson to her students: perfection is an enemy. If something is flawless then it is hiding its flaw from you. Holly plucked a wand-twig from the tree and weighed it in her palm. But she could not shake the wand: it was stuck there. She was cursed to hold it in her palm, presumably forever if the blightwood tree had its way. Holly was a sage enough wizard to remove the curse eventually, but it took some weeks to arrive at the solution. In the intervening period, she taught her lessons with a stony-face, grumpy temper, and a blightwood wand in her palm. She would point it threateningly at any student who dared to glance at her curse.

They were in the midst of astral projection or alterations of the mind when the fire swept through. Under the rubble, however, the rescue parties found something unusual. There was a room that wasn't on any plans, located beneath Arnuld's Sanctum. It wasn't particularly large: only a handful of wizards could have stood upright within it. But in that room was a plaque, lacquered to protect it from fire. On it was written "You have passed my trial. I have underestimated my fellow wizards. Take what is earned - Holly Arnuld". On the walls, around the plaque, was row upon row of wands. Splitbark and maple wands in their hundreds.

journal.text: The Brynmoor School of Magic fell to fire, and it didn't rally in another location. The school, it was said, had been losing money, and the wizards saw the fire as an opportunity to count their insurance money and cut any further losses. The students were left to apprentice elsewhere, if they could find the work, or practice their magic in other, ill-thought-out manners. Upon the death of a foremost wizard, an old dean of the School of Magic, a chest was wheeled out. Inside were hundreds of sticks, wrapped in cloth. The wizard's family believed them to be incense sticks or diffusers - scented with holly berries, as per a decoration on the stick's base. The family sold them for a single gold piece each. A poster was attached to the front of the chest with the words 'Fire Sale - Incense Sticks' . It is hard to describe the carnage that followed. The sticks were not incense but splitbark and maple wands, and those wands were intensely powerful. They were infused not with the smell of holly berries, but with the elements of fire, water, air and earth. When lit, they reacted explosively, and when held, they fired chaotically. Brynmoor was alight that night, and everyone had a different story of what happened to them, from stoves encased in rock to clothes blown clean off by air magic. Most of the wands were discarded or destroyed. But a few found their way into the hands of commoners - those who were not allowed, or could not afford, to practice magic. Street urchins, scullery maids, chimney sweeps. Each of them had the beginnings of magic in their hands.

journal.text: Holly Arnuld was buried with a Master Wand on her chest and her hand clasping it. Her last wishes, found in her desk, made it clear that the wand was to be placed as close to her heart as possible. A few other preparations were to be made, like the timing of the funeral, and her closest companions made them. As Holly was lowered into the ground at her funeral, her friends, fellow teachers and class raised their wands to the sky. It was respectful and somber, as was Brynmoor tradition. Just as the congregation was looking to disperse, the coffin shook, and the seams around the lid brightened. The coffin blew open and a flurry of fire spells exploded from the Master Wand. A nearby tree was set alight. Students had to use their jackets to stamp out fires on the lawn. Everyone claimed to hear cackling from the coffin, yet - when a brave teacher stooped over to have a look - Holly was still in repose, blackened a little with soot. It turned out that Holly was buried with a magical mechanism on her chest, timed to trigger at the end of the funeral. The cackling was the whirring and sputtering of the mechanism. The machine acted as a catalyst for the wand, and - well - you know the rest.

journal.text: Holly Arnuld , the famed 'wand wizard', only had one blood relative, yet she found out about this relative's existence entirely by accident. Frustrated at final-year students stealing her wands, Holly determined to discover a failsafe. She would create a spell that would respect the Bond of Blood: a spell that could be applied to her favourite wands to ensure only she used them. If someone without her blood tried to hold her Ancestral Wand, for example, then they would feel a burning pain. The magic worked, but not quite as intended. 'Perfection is the enemy', as she would say. Her Ancestral Wand was bound to Arnuld blood, but it had not chosen Holly as the one who should wield it. There was another Arnuld out there, in the wilds, and the Ancestral Wand stubbornly decided that it belonged to THEM. Holly hated that the next step was borrowed from a child's fairy tale, but there was no other choice. She invited people to come up and try to hold the wand. If they could do so without feeling pain, then she would recognise them as a relative and bequeath half of her estate. Hundreds of townsfolk tried, until a young orphan held the wand with no after-effect. Holly took her under her wing. The Ancestral Wand had a new owner. Holly Arnuld tinkered with the Bond of Blood spell over the years, creating a variant that would eventually be used in her memorial chamber: Arnuld's Sanctum.

journal.text: When Kuldra was no bigger than a terrorbird, the dragonkin Viika would play with her. They had bonded - the dragon and the seer. It is hard to imagine that this was the same Kuldra whose five heads would eventually loom over Ashenfall. Their early relationship had but one frosty moment. Viika's eyes glazed over and they grabbed a stick and thrust it into Kuldra's paw. Kuldra screamed and tried to rip the stick out, but it was a splinter that her teeth couldn't reach. It had retreated too far into her body. The playmates were pulled apart, with Viika screaming fragmented nonsense about "bringing a weapon to the world" and "I did what must be done, yet also did not". Kuldra was confused about the sudden betrayal. She retreated into the pile of rags that she had made into a nest. Later, Viika approached Kuldra with an upturned palm, their thoughts more lucid. They asked Kuldra for forgiveness, and Kuldra gave it happily. But while they returned to being friends, Kuldra was unable to remove the splinter. It itched and ached as it pushed further into her bloodstream.

It comes pre-segmented and it's made from some of the hardiest organic material known to mortalkind. You just need to kill the demon, twist the shoulder, sever a tendon, and Io - your very own Abyssal Whip... right? Wrong. Turns out, it's a bit more involved than you expected, and this "weapon" demonstrates that all too well. Still, not all is lost. Perhaps there is a way, a method, to turn this... Crafting a weapon from their remains symbolizes triumph against adversity or perhaps just hubris in its purest form. Infused with the hate of the demon, each whip crack generates unbearable pain. Victims find themselves overcome with suffering as the agony seeps into the wounds the whips leave behind. It is said that the whip even feeds on that misery, growing stronger with each life taken. The hate imbues the weapon with a desire to inflict more pain, and it grows stronger each time such a wish is granted. Or, so the legends say. Only one Wild Knight has ever chosen to wield the whip in vengeance against the demon for a fallen sibling. Her name is dust in the wind of history, but there are still creatures that hide in the shadows, afraid of the crack of her whip.
